probes.question: What does a vaccine do?
options: It kills the germs directly in the blood
It teaches the immune system to recognise a germ before the real infection
It swaps your white blood cells for new ones
It makes the body immune to every disease

probes.question: True or false: Jenner's 1796 experiment used cowpox material to protect against smallpox.

image.alt: A pastel portrait of Edward Jenner leaning on a tree, with a milkmaid and cows in the background.

panels.text: England, 1796. Edward Jenner suspects that people who catch cowpox, a much milder disease, are protected from smallpox.
On 14 May he takes pus from the cowpox blisters of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, and inoculates James Phipps, an eight-year-old, through two small cuts.
Phipps gets a fever but no full-blown infection. On 1 July Jenner injects him with smallpox material, and again no disease follows.

That is the idea behind vaccines today: a harmless version of a germ teaches the immune system to recognise it, so it can destroy the real one later. The word vaccine comes from Jenner's Latin for cowpox.
